title: Proposed 2023 budget and utility rates received
subtitle: Bill 23 adaptation plan, reserve fund changes, Uptown improvement grants, building and rental licensing fee increases
overview: Council received the proposed 2023 budget, which includes a 5.35% property tax increase. No budget approvals were sought; final decisions come in February after further meetings and a public session in January. Council approved the budget schedule {{vote:m11}}.

Council set 2023 water, sanitary and stormwater rates {{vote:m13}}, and approved a 12% rise in building standards fees {{vote:m9}} and 3.5% increases in rental housing and business licensing fees {{vote:m10}}. Interim spending authority for early 2023 was also approved {{vote:m7}}.

Council supported in principle a 10-point plan for adapting to Ontario's Bill 23 {{vote:m15}}. Staff warned of lost development charge revenue, added staffing pressure and possible effects on property taxes and infrastructure projects. Council also created a climate action reserve fund {{vote:m12}} and extended Uptown improvement grants through 2023 {{vote:m14}}.

decisions.detail: Council approved the budget schedule and received the proposed 2023 budget documents, which include a proposed 5.35% property tax increase, for consideration through February {{vote:m11}}.
Council approved 2023 water ($2.17/m3), sanitary ($2.69/m3) and stormwater rates effective January 1, 2023, and approved the 2024-2032 forecast in principle {{vote:m13}}.
Council supported in principle the 10-point plan for adapting to the province's More Homes Built Faster Act {{vote:m15}}.

decisions.item: Rental housing and business licensing fees
decisions.detail: Council approved 3.5% fee increases for 2023 for both programs and allowed the Rental Housing Reserve to stay in deficit until the end of 2027 {{vote:m10}}.
Council approved a 12% increase to all building standards fees and charges effective January 1, 2023 {{vote:m9}}.
Council created a Climate Action Reserve Fund, redirecting $918,000 of annual capital reserve funding to it, and approved a Community Benefits Charge reserve fund policy {{vote:m12}}.
Council extended the Uptown façade, major activity and parking exemption programs to December 31, 2023 and ended the city-wide COVID-relief CIP at the end of 2022 {{vote:m14}}.
Council approved 2023 interim operating spending authority not exceeding $50,910,000, equal to 25% of the 2022 operating budget {{vote:m7}}.

debate: On rental licensing fees, one councillor raised concern about the 3.5% increase given affordable housing pressures and floated a much smaller rise. Staff said a lower increase would deepen the reserve deficit, and removing planned tax support would worsen it. The alternative received no seconder and the motion passed as printed {{vote:m10}}.

Staff noted rent increases are set by the province, and that the licensing program funds safety inspections. A councillor said program quality and enforcement matter most for low-income renters. Another said they would resist tax-based support for the program in future years.

On building fees, a councillor asked whether the 12% rise should be monitored against Kitchener, which has held its fees. Staff said Waterloo will remain below Kitchener and that comparisons are reviewed regularly.

On Bill 23, staff said reduced development charges could leave a funding gap, with potential property tax impacts and trade-offs between growth and renewal projects. Staff also cited faster approval timelines and weaker conservation authority roles. A delegate described broad public concern and urged residents to comment on related proposals.

Councillors questioned the province's approach, noting the bill does not require affordable homes. One said property tax increases to cover lost revenue would be regressive. Staff said capital project deferrals will be reported on February 6.
